What it is
A Troy School District Board workshop presentation, 2026-2027 Budget Planning, dated January 13, 2026.

Amendment #1 takeaways
- FY24/25 'historical' funding was one-time categorical money that did not carry into the FY25/26 foundation; net -$5 million one-time replaced by a $5.5 million foundation increase
- TSD's aggregate FY25/26 increase was about $500,000 (~0.25%)
- Retirement and health-care costs once covered by the State shifted to the employer; inflation near 3%; costs continue to rise

Budget priorities
- Secure known expenditure obligations through 2029 for multi-year projections and labor stability
- Data-driven alignment of student support services, maximizing grant funds for literacy, math, and ELD interventions
- Reductions through attrition where feasible (95% of budget is people); reduction in force viewed through the lens of least impact on student achievement, with layoffs a last measure

Proposed timeline
- Jan 13 workshop (Amendment #1); CREC Jan 16; Feb 3 workshop (Plante Moran Cresa enrollment projections, Governor's Executive Budget); Mar 7 retreat (possible Amendment #2); April workshop (reduction recommendations); June regular meeting (Amendment #3, FY26-27 budget resolution, final RIF targets)

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Presented at the Troy School District Board Workshop on January 13, 2026, this deck addresses 2026-2027 budget planning.

On State Aid Amendment #1, the presentation cautions that although the prior year's funding was touted as 'historical,' FY24/25 funding was one-time categorical money that did not carry into the FY25/26 foundation: a net $5 million of one-time funding was replaced with a $5.5 million foundation increase in FY25/26. The aggregate increase for TSD in FY25/26 was approximately $500,000, amounting to about a 0.25% increase. Several prior-year categorical funds were rolled into the foundation, and retirement and health-care costs once covered by the State have been shifted to the employer. The final State Aid budget was not completed until well into SY25/26, limiting the district's ability to make late staffing adjustments; inflation remains around 3%, and costs are expected to keep rising.

Budget priority talking points fall into three areas. First, securing known expenditure obligations through 2029 to enable multi-year budget projections, staffing plans, strategic-planning alignment, and labor stability and morale. Second, data-driven alignment of student support services, maximizing grant funds to assign literacy, math, and English Language Development (ELD) interventions equitably and to provide a data-supported rationale for potential reductions. Third, reductions through attrition where feasible, a strategy used over the last three years to avoid layoffs through use of fund balance; the deck notes that 95% of the budget is people, that any reduction in force (RIF) would be viewed through the lens of least impact on student achievement, and that layoffs remain the last measure. A staffing-ratios document tracks FTE allocation across departments, with ELD and literacy specialists still in flux.

The proposed budget timeline runs: the January 13, 2026 workshop (Amendment #1, budget process and talking points, initial assumptions); the Michigan Consensus Revenue Estimating Conference (CREC) on January 16; a February 3 workshop featuring Plante Moran Cresa enrollment projections, with the Governor's Executive Budget due early February and the State of the State on February 25; a March 7 retreat with a possible Amendment #2 and House and Senate budget triangulation; an April workshop providing potential reduction recommendations; and a June regular meeting adopting Amendment #3 and the FY26-27 budget resolution with final RIF targets.

Finally, a School Finance Engagement Group (SFEG) will meet on January 21, February 10, March 10, April 14, and May 12, from 5:00 to 6:30 PM in the Services Board Room. Planned topics progress from an orientation to district demographics and school funding, through revenue and expenditure deep dives, ancillary funds and Bond/BSSF, to FY26/27 budget priorities and a stakeholder feedback opportunity. Board members are welcome to attend and will receive materials in advance.

A Troy School District Board workshop presentation (January 2026) updating the middle school mathematics program, grounded in NCTM's 2020 Catalyzing Change in Middle School Mathematics and prior May 2023 decisions.

- Stronger problem-solving and mathematical communication

- 93% find math class welcoming; 90% agree 'I know I can be good at math'; 79% feel prepared for the next level; 59% say lessons are 'just right'
- 45% do not enjoy learning math; 34% want more specific feedback; 24% find lessons too easy; 17% too hard
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Presented at a Troy School District Board Workshop in January 2026, this update reviews the middle school mathematics program and its progress since decisions made in May 2023. It frames the district's vision, drawing on NCTM's 2020 Catalyzing Change in Middle School Mathematics, that all students are doers of mathematics who develop deep understanding, learn to understand and critique the world through mathematics, and experience its wonder, joy, and beauty.

The May 2023 findings that prompted change were: (1) program data from the five years preceding COVID showed student performance slightly decreasing or stagnant, with cohort data showing a decrease in students reaching advanced and proficient and an increase in those not proficient; (2) students were not able to fluidly move between tracks in middle school; and (3) a need to explore task-based, inquiry-based instruction that builds procedural fluency through conceptual understanding. The resulting recommendation was to adopt the Illustrative Math curriculum, described as problem-based, aligned to Universal Design for Learning, with embedded supports for students with disabilities and English learners, extensions for students ready for more, built-in instructional routines, predictable lesson structure, and practice sets with cumulative review.

For course selection, families choose between Math 8, a natural transition from Math 7 covering linearity, functions, and geometry, and Honors Algebra 1, which embeds Math 8 standards into Algebra 1 with a focus on efficiency and mastery. In the spring of 7th grade, buildings host information nights and families engage with math teachers, considering problem-solving skills, communication of mathematical thinking, assessment feedback, and standardized test scores. Supports for all students include professional learning, enrichment materials embedded in Illustrative Math ('Are You Ready for More?'), math club and robotics, and traditional test-out opportunities offered every spring, allowing students to reach Algebra 1 by Grade 8 or earlier.

The district's monitoring goals are to see growth in the number of students scoring advanced or proficient on the M-STEP math assessment, PSAT, and SAT; to increase enrollment in and successful completion of Honors Algebra 1 in 8th grade; and to build problem-solving skills and communication of mathematical thinking, measured through M-STEP/PSAT/SAT and cohort data, benchmark and common assessments, enrollment in Algebra 1, and grades in higher-level mathematics.

May 2025 student perception data from 1,932 students report several celebrations: 93% said their math class is a welcoming place for everyone, 87% had lots of opportunities to interact, 88% agreed it is important to try rather than to get things right the first time, 90% agreed 'I know I can be good at math,' 79% feel prepared for the next level of math, and 59% said lessons are 'just right for them.' Challenges include 34% wanting more specific feedback on how to improve, 45% who do not enjoy learning math, 24% who found lessons too easy, and 17% who found them too hard. Accompanying student-voice quotes describe enjoying peer interaction, real-life examples, multiple ways to learn, and feeling confident to participate without being judged.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This narrative accompanies the annual updates to the Troy School District High School Course Description Book (CDB) for the 2026/2027 school year. The CDB shows course requirements and elective opportunities and is organized by department so students and families understand the offerings. It is described as a OneTroy document developed collaboratively by administrators and department heads from both high schools along with the Teaching and Learning team, and it is updated annually as part of the curriculum review process, with department teams determining where descriptions should be updated and where courses should be added or deleted.

The document then details the courses added for 2026/2027. AP Business with Personal Finance (Grades 9-12, full year, 1.0 credit) satisfies one credit of the math-related graduation requirement and introduces students to knowledge and skills for growing careers and managing money; developed with college faculty and industry leaders, it offers the opportunity to earn college credit and an employer-endorsed credential, and it meets the introductory requirement for students to potentially compete in DECA the following year.

AP Cybersecurity (Grades 9-12, full year, 1.0 credit) replaces and builds upon the previously offered Cybersecurity course and aligns with a college-level introductory cybersecurity course. Students learn about threats, vulnerabilities, and risk, and how risk can be mitigated through a defense-in-depth strategy across physical spaces, computer networks, devices, and data and applications. Content aligns with the National Initiative for Cybersecurity Education (NICE) Workforce Framework, and the course is part of the AP Career Kickstart group, offering an employer-endorsed credential.

AP Precalculus AB (Grades 9-12, full year, 1.0 credit) requires completion of Algebra 2 and replaces the previously offered Precalculus. It is described as a college-level course preparing students for calculus and STEM fields through the study of functions, modeling, and problem-solving, covering polynomial, rational, exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric functions, polar and parametric equations, and rates of change; students may take the AP Precalculus exam and are prepared for AP Calculus AB.

AP Precalculus BC (Grades 9-12, full year, 1.0 credit) also requires Algebra 2 and replaces the previously offered Honors Precalculus, covering the same major topics plus the additional content of limits and derivatives and vectors, and preparing students for AP Calculus BC.

Career Capstone (Grades 11-12, one semester, 1/2 credit) requires students to be a completer in a business pathway (Finance, BAMO, or Marketing). Described as a CTE Professional Capstone, it prepares students for college, careers, and professional environments; students build a professional identity through a resume, LinkedIn profile, and digital portfolio, engage in professional-based learning projects with business partners, and refine employability skills through interview practice, career coaching, and job-shadow opportunities, graduating with a professional toolkit supporting job applications, internships, apprenticeships, and postsecondary pathways.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Presented at the Troy School District Board of Education Workshop on January 13, 2026, this slide summarizes the 2026 updates to the High School Course Description Book (CDB) taking effect in the 2026/2027 school year; a companion narrative document provides the full course descriptions.

Seven new courses are added. AP Business with Personal Finance is new; AP Cybersecurity replaces the prior Cybersecurity course; AP Precalculus AB replaces Precalculus; and AP Precalculus BC replaces Honors Precalculus. Additional new offerings are Career Capstone, Mathematics of Tabletop Games, and Sports Officiating.

The 11th grade English program is restructured into two semester choices. In Semester 1, under the strand Literary Analysis in Reading; Writing about Reading, students choose one of Great American Stories, Contemporary American Literature, or American Dramas and Musicals. In Semester 2, under Writing with a Purpose and Exploring Mentor Texts, students choose one of Persuasive Writing, Writing Imaginative Fiction, or Writing Personal Memoirs.

Eleven courses that have not run in five years are removed: Political Science, Stories of Yourself and Others, Psychology 2, Conflicts of the 20th Century, Philosophy, Literature of Suspense, Science Fiction, Voices in Literature, Modern Shakespeare, Interior Design, and Stitchery.

Other changes noted include renaming Achievement Skills III to Integrated Studies III, an increase in math-related and NCAA course approvals, and a change in the course book's publication format from PDF to PaperTurn.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose: An agenda memo issued by Superintendent Richard M. Machesky, Ed.D., to the Troy Board of Education, setting the order of business for the Organizational Meeting held January 20, 2026. The memo lists six sequential items. First, the board elects an acting chairperson to conduct the meeting until the organizational business has been completed. Second, the acting chairperson appoints Judy Holmes to act as temporary secretary until the board's secretary is elected. Third, the acting chairperson declares nominations in order for president of the board of education, noting that nominations need not be supported, that a motion and support are made to close nominations, and that four votes are required for election. Fourth, the newly elected president declares nominations in order for vice president, following the same procedure. Fifth, the president declares nominations for secretary, and sixth, for treasurer, each following the same procedure. The document is purely procedural, governing the annual organization of the board and the election of its officers.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A Troy School District Board of Education resolution to opt in to Section 31aa of the 2025-2026 State School Aid Act, which allocates $321 million statewide for school safety and mental health and requires districts to accept a state comprehensive investigation and waive any privilege in the event of a mass casualty event. The Board declares the privilege-waiver requirement likely unconstitutional yet still opts in to secure the funding, ratifying the Superintendent's earlier conditional opt-in and limiting any waiver to mass casualty events occurring after receipt of funds through the end of the 2025-2026 fiscal year.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
A suggested resolution for the Troy Board of Education (County of Oakland, State of Michigan) to opt in to receive Section 31aa funds under the 2025-2026 State School Aid Act, considered as Business item 11.C. at the January 20, 2026 meeting.

Key facts
- The State School Aid Act and State budget for 2025-2026 were signed into law on October 7, 2025.
- Section 31aa allocates $321,000,000.00 statewide; districts must opt in to be eligible for their share.
- To receive funds, a district must submit to a state comprehensive investigation and affirmatively waive any privilege protecting information from disclosure after a mass casualty event.
- A Michigan Court of Claims order entered November 21, 2025 let districts that opted in by 11:59 p.m. December 4, 2025 rescind by 11:59 p.m. December 30, 2025.

Board position
The Board believes the requirement to waive any privilege is likely unconstitutional and, if enforced, an intolerable burden on its operation, but still desires the funds for school safety and mental health programs.

Resolution
- Declares the Board's interest to opt in.
- Ratifies the Superintendent's prior conditional opt-in and authorizes execution of future 31aa documents required by MDE.
- Limits any required waiver to a mass casualty event occurring after the District receives funds, through the end of the 2025-2026 fiscal year.
- Rescinds all conflicting resolutions.

Purpose
Secure the District's share of state safety and mental-health funding while narrowing the scope of the privilege waiver the Board considers constitutionally suspect. Closes with Secretary certification under the Open Meetings Act, 1976 PA 267.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Business item 11.C. at the Troy School District Board of Education's Organizational and Regular Meeting of January 20, 2026 (County of Oakland, State of Michigan), presenting a suggested resolution to opt in to receive Section 31aa funds. The resolution recites that the State School Aid Act and State budget for the 2025-2026 school year were signed into law on October 7, 2025, and that Section 31aa allocates a total of $321,000,000.00 to all districts statewide, with districts required to opt in to be eligible for their share.

Conditions of funding: To receive Section 31aa money, a district, intermediate district, nonpublic school, or the Michigan Schools for the Deaf and Blind must agree to be subject to a comprehensive investigation and must affirmatively agree to waive any privilege that might otherwise protect information from disclosure in the event of a mass casualty event. The comprehensive investigation would assess the circumstances of the event, including emergency response effectiveness, compliance with safety protocols, communication procedures, and any factors contributing to the incident. The governor designates the investigating person or entity, which may include state law enforcement agencies, independent review boards, or specially appointed task forces, with authority to access relevant district records and data, interview witnesses and district personnel, and issue findings and recommendations. A detailed report of findings must be submitted to the governor and relevant legislative committees within 90 days following the conclusion of the investigation, including recommendations for preventing future incidents and improving school safety protocols.

Definition: A mass casualty event means an incident occurring on school grounds or at a school-sponsored event that (i) results in significant injuries to not fewer than 3 individuals, (ii) results in fatalities, (iii) exceeds the normal emergency-response resources of the jurisdiction, or (iv) produces a sudden and timely surge of injured individuals necessitating emergency services.

Procedural timeline: An order of the Michigan Court of Claims entered November 21, 2025 provided that a district opting in to receive 31aa funds by 11:59 p.m. on December 4, 2025 could subsequently rescind that opt-in decision by 11:59 p.m. on December 30, 2025.

Board position and resolved clauses: The Board states its belief that the requirement to waive any privilege is likely unconstitutional and, if enforced, would be an intolerable burden on its ability to operate, but nonetheless desires Section 31aa funds for school safety and mental health programs. The resolution declares the Board's interest to opt in; recognizes that the Superintendent has already acted in the Board's best interest by conditionally opting in to receive the funds; and authorizes the Superintendent to execute future 31aa documents as required by the Michigan Department of Education (MDE). To the extent allowed by law, any required waiver or consent is limited to a mass casualty event occurring after the District receives Section 31aa funds through the end of the 2025-2026 fiscal year, and applies only for that fiscal year or any shorter duration consistent with law. All resolutions and parts of resolutions that conflict with this one are rescinded. The document closes with certification language by the Secretary of the Board of Education attesting that the resolution was adopted at the January 20, 2026 meeting, held with public notice given under the Open Meetings Act, 1976 PA 267, as amended.

Consideration item 4.E. at the Troy School District Board of Education's organizational meeting of January 20, 2026, presenting a suggested resolution to establish the District's fund depositories and investment authority. The recommended action is acceptance of the resolution, which the Board adopts for the period January through December 2026 and directs to be incorporated in its entirety as part of the official Board minutes.

The resolution recites that public monies belonging to or held for the State, County, or other political units come into the hands of the Treasurer of Troy School District, and that Michigan law requires the Board to designate by resolution one or more banks for the deposit of all public monies, including tax monies. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A budget presentation for the Troy School District delivered to the Board of Education on January 20, 2026 by presenter Dan Trudel, CPA, covering the 2025-2026 General Fund Budget Amendment #1. The presentation frames four categories of adjustment: categorical funding adjusted to reflect the state aid status report; federal grant funding adjusted to reflect final allocations; ISD-related funding sources adjusted to reflect final allocations; and purchased services, salaries, and benefits budgets adjusted to reflect anticipated final expenditures.

Revenue expectation changes from the original budget include enrollment falling from 12,074.00 to 12,071.23 (a decrease of 2.77) while the foundation figure rises from $130,230,164 to $130,788,472 (up $558,308). Key MPSERS line changes: 27L(4) goes from $0 to $1,326,153; 147A(1) is eliminated from $1,007,246 to $0; and 35(A) Early Literacy drops from $176,655 to $0. On MPSERS context, in Fiscal Year 2025 the state provided 147a(4) funds of $5,055,278 to offset retirement expenses as a one-time categorical payment that does not roll into the future foundation allowance and was eliminated for FY2026. For FY2026 the state eliminated 147a(1) at the last minute (-$1,007,246); employees are no longer contributing the 3% healthcare premium, which the employer has absorbed this year; pension UAAL expenditures for districts were reduced by 5.75%; healthcare premium subsidy expenditures increased by 2.58%; and pension normal cost expenditures increased by up to 1.72%.

The General Fund summary compares the original 2025-2026 budget to Amendment #1: revenues rise from $190,545,984 to $197,935,255 (a $7,389,271 increase); expenditures rise from $194,285,613 to $203,763,818 (a $9,478,205 increase); the change in fund balance moves from -$3,739,629 to -$6,003,563 (a $2,263,934 larger draw); the beginning fund balance is $32,979,691 rising to $33,713,795 (+$734,104); and the ending fund balance falls from $29,240,062 to $27,710,232 (-$1,529,830), taking the fund balance percentage from 15.05% to 13.59% (down 1.46%).

Notable revenue adjustments (change from original budget) include: MPSERS 27L(4) +$1,326,153 (one-time funding added after the original budget was adopted); Clean Bus Sec. 74B +$961,330 (grant funds for two additional EV buses); 31aa carryover +$1,389,660 and a new 31aa allocation +$576,658 (state increased the allocation); property tax collections +$996,304; At Risk Sec. 31A +$355,808; transfers in +$600,000 (from $1.4 million to $2.0 million); state aid adjustments +$845,368 (actuals near $850,000 versus a conservative $5,000 budget); Transportation 22L +$450,683; ISD PA-18 Special Education +$321,230; State Aid Special Education +$249,126 (final SE-4096 reimbursement); Bilingual Sec. 41 +$123,690; Enrollment Stabilization State Aid +$274,098; and MPSERS 147A(1) -$1,007,246 - for a total revenue change of $7,462,862. Notable expenditure adjustments include: total grant adjustments +$1,920,496; purchased services +$411,047; salary adjustment +$2,928,213 (reflecting actual attrition); retirement adjustment +$3,612,635 (actual attrition plus unanticipated increases in employer contribution rates); and 147c(1) MPSERS +$605,680 - for a total expenditure change of $9,478,071. The presentation also notes corresponding adjustments to other funds to reflect anticipated actuals.

What it is
A board financial exhibit comparing how eight comparable metro-Detroit districts allocate operating spending, with each function shown as a percentage of that district's total budget. Every line is color-coded from the darkest shade (highest percentage among the districts) to the lightest (lowest).

Districts compared
Troy, Rochester Community Schools, Bloomfield Hills Schools, Birmingham Public Schools, Avondale School District, Utica Community Schools, Warren Consolidated Schools, and Novi Public Schools.

Troy's allocation (share of budget)
- Instructional Expenditures: 65.75%
- Pupil Support Services: 8.14%
- Instructional Staff Support Services: 6.22%
- General Administration: 1.16%
- School Administration: 5.16%
- Business Services: 0.87%
- Operations and Maintenance: 7.74%
- Transportation: 2.35%
- Central & Other Support Services: 2.02%
- Community & Facilities: 0.59%

Context
Troy leads all eight districts in instructional share (65.75%), ahead of Novi (64.75%) and Avondale (64.48%); Warren Consolidated is lowest at 57.93%. Troy posts the lowest transportation share (2.35%) and among the lowest shares for operations and maintenance (7.74%), business services (0.87%), and community and facilities (0.59%). To give the Board a benchmark of Troy's spending priorities relative to comparable districts, highlighting the district's relatively high instructional investment and lean transportation and support overhead.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A board financial exhibit titled "District Comparisons - Operating Expenditures," presented at the January 20, 2026 Organizational and Regular Meeting, benchmarks how Troy School District allocates its operating budget against seven comparable districts: Rochester Community Schools, Bloomfield Hills Schools, Birmingham Public Schools, Avondale School District, Utica Community Schools, Warren Consolidated Schools, and Novi Public Schools. Each expenditure function is shown as a percentage of the district's total budget, and every line is color-coded from the darkest shade (highest percentage among the districts) to the lightest (lowest).

Troy's operating expenditures break down as follows: Instructional Expenditures 65.75%; Pupil Support Services 8.14%; Instructional Staff Support Services 6.22%; General Administration 1.16%; School Administration 5.16%; Business Services 0.87%; Operations and Maintenance 7.74%; Transportation 2.35%; Central & Other Support Services 2.02%; and Community & Facilities 0.59%. The columns sum to 100%.

Across the eight districts, Troy commits the largest share of its budget to instruction at 65.75%, followed by Novi (64.75%) and Avondale (64.48%); Warren Consolidated devotes the smallest instructional share at 57.93%, with Bloomfield Hills (58.56%) and Rochester (58.82%) also below 59%. Comparative ranges for other functions include Pupil Support Services from Utica's 6.68% to Warren's 11.43%; Instructional Staff Support Services from Avondale's 3.75% to Novi's 7.97%; General Administration from Utica's 0.40% to Bloomfield Hills' 1.21%; Operations and Maintenance from Novi's 4.92% to Birmingham's 10.22%; Transportation from Troy's 2.35% (the lowest in the group) to Rochester's 4.18%; and Community & Facilities from Avondale's 0.12% to Utica's 6.19%.

Relative to peers, Troy stands out for directing the highest proportion of spending to instruction while running the lowest transportation share and among the lowest shares for operations and maintenance (7.74%), business services (0.87%), and community and facilities (0.59%). Its general administration (1.16%) and school administration (5.16%) shares sit toward the higher end of the comparison group. The exhibit contains no dollar amounts, enrollment figures, or narrative text - it is strictly a percentage-of-budget allocation comparison intended to show the Board where Troy's spending priorities differ from neighboring districts.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
An informational report to the Troy Board of Education describing the annual updates to the district's High School Course Description Book (CDB) for the 2026/2027 school year. The CDB documents course requirements and elective opportunities and is organized by department so that students and families can understand the offerings. The report characterizes the CDB as a 'OneTroy' document developed collaboratively by administrators and department heads from both high schools together with the Teaching and Learning team, and notes that it is updated annually as part of the district's curriculum-review process, with department teams determining where descriptions should change and where courses should be added or deleted.

The document details courses added for 2026/2027. AP Business with Personal Finance (Grades 9-12, full year, 1.0 credit) satisfies one credit of the math-related graduation requirement; developed with college faculty and industry leaders, it offers the opportunity to earn college credit and an employer-endorsed credential and meets the introductory requirement for students to compete in DECA the following year. AP Cybersecurity (Grades 9-12, full year, 1.0 credit) replaces and builds upon the previously offered Cybersecurity course; it covers common threats, vulnerabilities, risk, and defense-in-depth mitigation across physical spaces, computer networks, devices, data, and applications; it is part of the AP Career Kickstart group of courses, aligns with the National Initiative for Cybersecurity Education (NICE) Workforce Framework, and offers an employer-endorsed credential.

AP Precalculus AB (Grades 9-12, full year, 1.0 credit) requires completion of Algebra 2, replaces the previously offered Precalculus, and prepares students for the AP Precalculus exam and AP Calculus AB, covering polynomial, rational, exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric functions, polar and parametric equations, and rates of change. AP Precalculus BC (Grades 9-12, full year, 1.0 credit) likewise requires Algebra 2 and replaces the previously offered Honors Precalculus; it covers the same major topics plus the additional content of limits and derivatives and vectors, preparing students for AP Calculus BC. Career Capstone (Grades 11-12, one semester, 1/2 credit) is open to students who are completers in a business pathway (Finance, BAMO, or Marketing); described as the CTE Professional Capstone, it is a culminating experience in which students build a professional identity through a resume, LinkedIn profile, and digital portfolio, engage in professional-based learning projects with business partners, and practice employability skills via formal interviews, career coaching, and job-shadow opportunities, graduating with a professional toolkit that supports job applications, internships, apprenticeships, and postsecondary pathways.

The extracted text ends within the entry for an added English 11 Semester 1 course ('Literary Analysis in Reading; Writing about Reading'), so the complete roster of additions - and any courses deleted for 2026/2027 - is not fully captured in this excerpt. Overall, the update reflects a continued emphasis on Advanced Placement offerings (business with personal finance, cybersecurity, and a restructured precalculus sequence aligned to the College Board's AP Precalculus framework) and on career-and-technical education capstone experiences within the district's two high schools.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Presented at the Troy School District Organizational and Regular Meeting of the Board of Education on January 20, 2026, this workshop slide summarizes the 2026 updates to the High School Course Description Book (CDB) taking effect in the 2026/2027 school year.

Seven new courses are added. AP Business with Personal Finance is new; AP Cybersecurity replaces the prior Cybersecurity course; AP Precalculus AB replaces Precalculus; and AP Precalculus BC replaces Honors Precalculus. Additional new offerings are Career Capstone, Mathematics of Tabletop Games, and Sports Officiating.

The 11th grade English program is restructured into two semester choices. In Semester 1, under the strand Literary Analysis in Reading; Writing about Reading, students choose one of Great American Stories, Contemporary American Literature, or American Dramas and Musicals. In Semester 2, under Writing with a Purpose and Exploring Mentor Texts, students choose one of Persuasive Writing, Writing Imaginative Fiction, or Writing Personal Memoirs.

Eleven courses that have not run in five years are removed: Political Science, Stories of Yourself and Others, Psychology 2, Conflicts of the 20th Century, Philosophy, Literature of Suspense, Science Fiction, Voices in Literature, Modern Shakespeare, Interior Design, and Stitchery.

Other changes noted include renaming Achievement Skills III to Integrated Studies III, an increase in math-related and NCAA course approvals, and a change in the course book's publication format from PDF to PaperTurn.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A literacy curriculum selection timeline outlining Troy School District's K-8 English/language-arts adoption process from January 2026 through a planned board recommendation in April 2027. The plan sequences staff and parent surveys, academic-data analysis, formation of a literacy leadership team, creation of an evaluation rubric, selection of materials to pilot, a spring 2026 community night, and district PD days, culminating in pilots that conclude in February 2027 and a synthesized curricular recommendation in March 2027.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
A month-by-month literacy curriculum selection timeline for Troy School District's K-8 adoption process, spanning January 2026 through April 2027.

Key milestones
- January 2026: Staff and parent communications and surveys; process check-ins with principal groups; begin vendor coordination for material previews and orientations.
- February 2026: Open code surveys and analyze academic data; board communication on the curriculum-adoption administrative regulation and adoption timeline; literacy leadership team meets to review data and draft a vision; determine pilot process parameters.
- March 2026: Literacy leadership team creates a rubric/evaluation tool; district PD day familiarizes larger groups with the work to date.
- April 2026: Literacy leadership team previews and selects materials to pilot; finalizes pilot timeline, participating classrooms, and data to collect.
- May 2026: Order materials at pilot scale; schedule vendors for August PD; host a community night for caretakers; communicate the vision and pilot details to the board; PD-day check-in for pilot teams.
- August 2026: District PD day for continued learning and pilot vendor training.
- October 2026: District PD day for follow-up PD and pilot rollout planning.
- February 2027: Pilots conclude.
- March 2027: District PD day to synthesize a curricular recommendation.
- April 2027: Board recommendation.

Purpose
To structure a transparent, data- and stakeholder-informed selection and piloting process before a final board recommendation.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A literacy curriculum selection timeline mapping the Troy School District's K-8 English/language-arts adoption process month by month from January 2026 through April 2027.

In January 2026, the district plans staff and parent communications and surveys, process check-ins with principal groups, and the beginning of vendor coordination for material previews and orientations. In February 2026, work includes opening code surveys and analyzing academic data; a board communication covering the curriculum adoption process administrative regulation and the literacy adoption timeline; a literacy leadership team meeting to preview the timeline, review academic and survey data, engage in common learning, and draft a vision; and determination of the pilot process parameters.

In March 2026, the literacy leadership team meets to create a rubric/evaluation tool, and a district professional development (PD) day familiarizes larger groups with the learning and steps the literacy team has already engaged in - previewing the timeline, reviewing academic and survey data, common learning, vision, and rubric, and previewing the parameters of the pilot process. In April 2026, the literacy leadership team previews materials and selects those to be piloted, and finalizes the pilot timeline, participating classrooms, and the data to be collected.

In May 2026, the district plans to order materials at pilot scale and schedule possible vendors for August PD; host a community night for caretakers to hear the research and vision process, interact with materials if available, and listen to the upcoming pilot process, with an opportunity for stakeholders to provide feedback; communicate the vision and pilot details to the board; and hold a district PD day check-in for pilot teams to further clarify pilots. In August 2026, a district PD day covers continued learning and pilot vendor training, and in October 2026 a district PD day provides follow-up PD and planning time for pilot rollouts.

The pilots conclude in February 2027. In March 2027, a district PD day synthesizes a curricular recommendation, and in April 2027 the board recommendation is scheduled. The timeline thus builds from surveys and data analysis through team-developed evaluation tools, material selection, community engagement, and classroom piloting toward a final board-level curricular recommendation.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: An administrative regulation defining the Troy School District's process for selecting or developing new instructional materials, developed in 2025 under the direction of Oakland Schools. It applies to essential curricular materials — math, science, social studies, and English, the courses required for grade progression — and establishes a four-phase adoption process led by the Director of Teaching & Learning through a Curriculum Review Committee (CRC). The phases move from committee formation through research and vision, piloting, and adoption with professional-development support, with board updates and community input built in.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
- An administrative regulation (dated December 17, 2025) documenting the Troy School District's curriculum adoption process, developed in 2025 under the direction of Oakland Schools.
- Applies to essential curricular materials: math, science, social studies, and English, the courses required for grade progression.

The four phases
- Phase 1 - Establish a Curriculum Review Committee: The Director of Teaching & Learning notifies stakeholders and forms a CRC including a curriculum and instruction specialist, teachers, and administrators representing general education, special education, and English Language Development. The Director serves as chairperson and the board is updated on the timeline.
- Phase 2 - Research and Vision: The CRC gathers perception data from teachers, administrators, caregivers, and students; analyzes district data; studies research and peer districts; drafts a vision statement; and builds an evaluation tool aligned to the strategic plan and to board policy covering students with disabilities and gifted students.
- Phase 3 - Explore and Pilot: The CRC scores and pilots materials (writing its own if none qualify), hosts a caregiver community night, updates the board, and presents a final recommendation with a professional-development plan for board approval.
- Phase 4 - Adopt and Support Implementation: Roll out the adopted curriculum with job-embedded coaching, classroom visits, and district-wide collaboration, reviewing data to adjust practices.

Purpose
- Standardize how the district researches, pilots, and adopts core instructional materials with stakeholder input and board oversight.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
The Troy School District's Curriculum Adoption Process Administrative Regulation, dated December 17, 2025, documents the district's standardized procedure for selecting or developing new instructional materials. The process was developed in 2025 under the direction of Oakland Schools and applies specifically to essential curricular materials, defined as math, science, social studies, and English, the courses the district requires for grade progression.

The regulation establishes a four-phase adoption process. In Phase 1 (Establish a Curriculum Review Committee), the Director of Teaching & Learning communicates with stakeholders about the upcoming adoption and forms a Curriculum Review Committee (CRC) for the designated content area. The CRC includes a curriculum and instruction specialist, teachers, and administrators representing general education, special education, and English Language Development, with the Director of Teaching & Learning serving as chairperson. The CRC develops a timeline covering the phases of research and vision, explore and pilot, and adopt and support implementation, and the board is updated on the anticipated process.

Phase 2 (Research and Vision) directs the CRC to gather stakeholder perception data from teachers, administrators, caregivers, and students when appropriate; analyze district data to identify strengths and needs within the content area; and learn best instructional practices by reviewing rigorous research, learning from peer districts, and partnering with experts. Based on this work, the CRC develops a vision statement for the content area and develops a tool for evaluating instructional materials that aligns with the research findings and the district's strategic plan. Per board policy, the curriculum must provide opportunities for students with disabilities as well as students considered gifted.

Phase 3 (Explore and Pilot) has the CRC evaluate potential materials and determine what to pilot, with the number of pilots based on how well materials score on the evaluation tool. If the CRC does not find existing resources that meet the evaluation criteria or the breadth of required state standards, it initiates planning to write its own curriculum or supplementary curriculum. The CRC determines the pilot timeline, logistics, participating classrooms, and data to be collected, and hosts a community night for caretakers to hear the research and vision process, interact with materials, and learn about the pilot, with an opportunity to provide feedback. The board receives an update, the pilot is implemented with job-embedded coaching and support for analyzing data, and the CRC then determines its recommended districtwide material and a professional-development plan and presents its final recommendation to the board for approval. Upon approval, the decision is communicated to all stakeholders and the resource is made available for caretakers to review, along with highlights of the curriculum, in a public setting.

Phase 4 (Adopt and Support Implementation) calls for implementing the new curriculum with the proposed professional-development plan, including options such as job-embedded coaching, classroom visits, and district-wide collaboration, and reviewing qualitative and quantitative data to adjust practices and provide additional professional learning as needed.

What it is
- A slide presentation to the Troy Board of Education explaining a proposed regional enhancement millage for Oakland County, tied to an August 4, 2026 election.

- Cost: about $300 per year on a Troy home valued at $400,000 (taxable value $200,000).
- Collection begins December 2026.

Comparisons and projections
- Nine counties already levy enhancement millages (44% of MI students), including Wayne (1.9812 mills, ~$360/student), Macomb (1.8305 mills, ~$400/student), Charlevoix-Emmet (0.953), Kalamazoo (1.4968), Kent (0.8578), Midland (1.5), Monroe (0.9866), Muskegon (0.9749), and Ottawa (0.8616).

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A Troy Board of Education workshop presentation, titled Enhancement Millage / August 4, 2026, explaining a proposed Oakland County regional enhancement millage. The deck reviews that since Proposal A in 1994 the state controls school funding, with a regional enhancement millage as the one exception: constituent school districts can request that a proposal be placed before voters, districts representing at least 51% of the total student population must submit affirmative requests to Oakland Schools expressing consideration, and the measure must be proposed and pass or fail on a countywide basis. If approved, the money is collected by the ISD and distributed equally to all public school districts and public school academies on a per-pupil basis, with each district retaining local control over how the money is spent.

The presentation states that nine Michigan counties already levy an enhancement millage, covering about 44% of the state's students: Wayne County (1.9812 mills, approximately $360 per student; approved 2016, renewed November 2020 and November 2024), Macomb County (1.8305 mills, approximately $400 per student; approved March 2020), Charlevoix-Emmet (0.953 mills), Kalamazoo (1.4968 mills), Kent (0.8578 mills), Midland (1.5 mills), Monroe (0.9866 mills), Muskegon (0.9749 mills), and Ottawa (0.8616 mills).

The proposal itself is 1.5 mills levied over six years, to be decided at a Tuesday, August 4, 2026 election. It would generate approximately $781 per pupil annually, roughly $4,686 per pupil over six years, for each Oakland County public student. It would cost approximately $300 per year on a Troy home valued at $400,000 (taxable value of $200,000). If successful, millage collection would begin in December 2026.

A year-by-year projection shows per-pupil revenue rising from $728.04 in Year 1 to $748.42, $769.38, $790.92, $813.07, and $835.84 in Year 6, with total revenue growing from $125.8 million in Year 1 to $129.3M, $132.9M, $136.7M, $140.5M, and $144.4M in Year 6.

On the timeline, local resolutions must be adopted within a 180-day period and transmitted to Oakland Schools; the Oakland Schools Board of Education then adopts a resolution certifying the text of the ballot proposal to the Oakland County Clerk (the School District Election Coordinator), with copies to local clerks and other affected county clerks, immediately after adoption. The deck references a Michigan School Board Association case-study presentation, Enhancement Millages: Successes, Challenges, Planning for the Future, citing Kent ISD, East Grand Rapids Public Schools, and Rockford Public Schools, along with a slide on cost outpacing funding and a slide on impact to teachers, the district, and students over the six years. The closing slide, Resolution: Let Voters Decide, states that the board's resolution is not an endorsement of the millage itself, that the board believes in empowering the community to make informed decisions, and that allowing voters to decide ensures democratic participation and transparency.

What it is
- A board brief laying out why Troy would pursue a countywide enhancement millage, what such a millage is, and the board's role in acting on the resolution.

Why pursue it
- School costs are rising faster than state foundation funding, which has not kept pace with inflation, and future state budgets do not suggest increases in line with obligations.
- District pressures cited: staff attraction/retention, rising third-party contract costs, retirement and insurance cost shifts from the state, federal underfunding of IDEA and Title, safety/security needs, and growing academic and social-emotional needs.

Mechanism
- Since Proposal A (1994), funding is largely state-controlled; a regional enhancement millage is one of the only ways to supplement per-pupil funding. Proposed and voted countywide; funds collected by Oakland Schools and distributed per pupil to districts and academies, with each local board controlling use. If not approved, no change to current funding.

The proposal
- Election August 4, 2026; 1.5 mills; 6-year term.
- About $781 per pupil annually; about $4,686 over six years; about $150 per year on a $200,000 home; first collection December 2026.

Context
- Oakland County has no enhancement millage; nine Michigan counties do (~44% of K-12 students), notably Wayne, Macomb, Kent, Monroe, Midland, and Kalamazoo.

Potential local uses
- Staff recruitment/retention, general-fund stabilization, special-education relief, student wellness supports (counselors and social workers), safety/security, literacy and math specialists, reducing cost shifts (pay-to-participate, club fees), and transportation/start-time challenges.

Board's role
- Not a vote on whether the millage passes, but whether to give voters the chance to decide and place the question on the August 2026 ballot — a governance, not advocacy, action.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A briefing document prepared for the Troy School Board explaining why the district would pursue a countywide regional enhancement millage, what such a millage is, and the board's role in acting on the resolution. The brief argues that school costs continue to rise faster than state foundation funding, that foundation increases have not kept pace with inflation, and that future state budgets do not suggest foundation increases in line with district obligations. It lists district pressures including attracting and retaining staff, rising third-party contract costs, the shifting of retirement and insurance costs from the state to districts, the federal government's failure to fund IDEA and Title programs, increased safety and security measures, and increased student academic and social-emotional needs.

On mechanics, the brief explains that since Proposal A in 1994 school funding is largely state-controlled, and a regional enhancement millage is one of the only mechanisms districts may use to supplement per-pupil funding. It must be proposed and voted on countywide; if approved, funds are collected by Oakland Schools and distributed per pupil to all public school districts and public school academies, with each local board controlling how the funds are used. If not approved, there is no change to current funding.

The brief stresses that the Troy Board's action allows a countywide question to appear on the ballot and does not represent support or opposition to the proposal — it is a governance decision, not an advocacy action, simply ensuring voters have the opportunity to decide. It notes Oakland County currently has no enhancement millage, while nine counties across Michigan already have one in place, representing approximately 44% of Michigan K-12 students; most notably Wayne, Macomb, Kent, Monroe, Midland, and Kalamazoo Counties have used an enhancement millage for multiple years.

The proposal overview lists an election date of August 4, 2026, a rate of 1.5 mills, and a six-year term, with an estimated impact if approved of approximately $781 per pupil annually, approximately $4,686 per pupil over six years, and approximately $150 per year on a $200,000 home; first collection could take place in December 2026. The brief emphasizes that the proposal provides local flexibility rather than mandates, and lists potential local uses co-determined with administration and the board: supporting staff recruitment and retention, stabilizing general fund budgets, relieving the pressure of special education funding on the general fund, enhancing student wellness supports (including counselor and social work capacity the district has been expanding), improving safety and security, maintaining and strengthening district programming such as literacy and math specialists, reducing cost shifts from the district to the community (for example pay-to-participate and club fees), and addressing transportation-related challenges such as school start times.

The brief closes by restating the board member's role: the board is not voting on whether the millage should pass, but on whether Oakland County voters should be given the opportunity to decide and whether the question should be placed on the August 2026 ballot, an action supporting the board's focus on transparency and public participation. It frames the resolution as keeping the decision where it belongs, with the voters, and as the only viable option school districts maintain to raise resources that support general fund operations.

What it is
The full formal resolution (agenda item 8.A) for adoption by the Troy School District Board of Education at its February 24, 2026 regular meeting (7:00 p.m.), requesting a regional enhancement millage election. It is drafted for inclusion in the official minutes, with blank lines for members present/absent and the mover/supporter.

Legal basis
Section 705 of the Revised School Code of 1976, as amended (MCL 380.705), lets an intermediate school district (ISD) levy a regional enhancement property tax of up to 3 mills - if approved by ISD electors - to enhance state and local funding for local school operating purposes. Proceeds are distributed to constituent districts on a per-pupil basis.

The request
- Asks Oakland Schools ISD to submit a proposal of 1.50 mills for six years, 2026-2031 inclusive.
- To be placed on the August 4, 2026 school election ballot, per Exhibit A ballot wording (subject to Oakland Schools' finalization).
- The Superintendent is directed to deliver a certified copy to the Secretary of the Oakland Schools Board.

Rationale
Wayne and Macomb County ISDs already levy voter-approved enhancement millages supporting reduced class sizes, enhanced programs, improved safety, and staff retention - benefits Oakland County does not currently receive.

Contingency
The question goes to voters only if constituent districts representing a majority of combined membership request it on or before March 31, 2026. Conflicting resolutions are rescinded. Certified as adopted in compliance with the Open Meetings Act (Act 267, P.A. 1976).
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
The full, formal resolution presented as agenda item 8.A for adoption at the February 24, 2026 regular meeting (7:00 p.m.) of the Troy School District Board of Education, County of Oakland, State of Michigan. Titled 'Resolution Requesting Regional Enhancement Millage Election,' it is formatted for the official minutes, with blank fields for members present and absent and for the members offering and supporting the resolution.

Legal framework: The resolution rests on Section 705 of the Revised School Code of 1976, as amended (MCL 380.705). Section 705 provides for the levy of a regional enhancement property tax by an intermediate school district (ISD), at a rate not to exceed 3 mills, to enhance other state and local funding for local school operating purposes, if approved by a majority of the ISD's electors. Proceeds are paid to each constituent school district (including eligible public school academies) on a per-pupil basis. A constituent district may request its ISD to submit the question to voters, and the ISD is required to do so if it receives requests from constituent districts representing a majority of combined membership as of the most recent membership count date.

Rationale (WHEREAS clauses): The resolution notes that the intermediate school districts in both Wayne and Macomb counties are currently authorized to levy voter-approved regional enhancement millages, providing benefits that may include reduced class sizes, enhanced program offerings, improved school safety, and increased staff retention and attraction - benefits Oakland County does not currently receive. It states that Oakland County residents deserve the opportunity to provide competitive educational opportunities comparable to neighboring Wayne and Macomb counties, and that voters should be able to decide whether to support such efforts.

Operative provisions (NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED): (1) The District requests that Oakland Schools submit to its electors the question of a regional enhancement millage proposal for 1.50 mills for a period of six (6) years, 2026 to 2031 inclusive, at the school election to be held August 4, 2026, per a ballot proposal substantially in the form of Exhibit A. (2) The District approves the Exhibit A ballot wording, subject to revision and finalization by Oakland Schools. (3) The Superintendent is authorized and directed to deliver a certified copy of the resolution to the Secretary of the Board of Education of Oakland Schools. (4) The resolution is only a request; the proposal will be submitted to voters only if Oakland Schools receives requests from constituent districts representing a majority of combined membership on or before March 31, 2026. (5) All resolutions and parts of resolutions in conflict are rescinded.

Certification: The resolution includes AYES and NAYS lines, is 'declared adopted,' and carries the Secretary's certification that the meeting was conducted and noticed in full compliance with the Open Meetings Act (Act 267, Public Acts of Michigan, 1976). Exhibit A, the Oakland Schools Intermediate School District Regional Enhancement Millage Proposal ballot language, is attached (the extracted text of Exhibit A is cut off).

The RFP resulted in three bids, and T&M Asphalt is recommended as the low-qualified bidder. Carson notes that T&M has successfully performed similar work for Troy School District and other school districts in Metro Detroit, and that post-bid interviews were conducted to verify bid accuracy and thoroughness.

The financial recommendation is a total project cost award of $289,131.00, comprising T&M Asphalt Paving, Inc.'s base bid of $272,765.00 plus a 6% contingency of $16,366.00. Carson requests approval of this total, upon which a purchase order will be issued. Funding for the purchase will come from the Capital Projects Fund.

On timing, the memo states the intent to start the project in spring 2026 when weather permits, performing as much scope as possible without disrupting daily school programs and functions, with completion expected before the 2026-27 school year commences. The memo is copied to Donna Havrilla in the Business Department and to the Purchasing Department file. Together with the three-bidder bid tabulation and the board resolution, this memo forms the documentation package for the Athens auxiliary parking lot award.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Board presentation on a proposed Oakland County regional enhancement millage set for the August 4, 2026 ballot. Under Michigan's 1994 Proposal A, the enhancement millage is the sole route for districts to raise additional operating revenue; it requires districts representing at least 51% of county student enrollment to request it, is decided county-wide, and is distributed by the ISD equally per pupil. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
Informational presentation to the Troy Board of Education on a proposed regional (county-wide) enhancement millage for Oakland County, targeted for the August 4, 2026 election.

Background
- Since Proposal A (1994) the state controls school operating funding; the regional enhancement millage is the one exception.
- Districts representing at least 51% of the county's student population must ask Oakland Schools (the ISD) to place it on the ballot; it passes or fails county-wide, not by community.
- Revenue is collected by the ISD and distributed equally per pupil; each district controls how its share is spent.

The proposal
- 1.5 mills levied over 6 years; collection would begin December 2026.
- About $781 per pupil annually (roughly $4,686 per pupil over six years) for each Oakland County public-school student.
- Cost about $300/year on a Troy home valued at $400,000 (taxable value $200,000).

Context
- Nine Michigan counties already levy one, including Wayne (1.9812 mills, ~$360/student), Macomb (1.8305 mills, ~$400/student), Kalamazoo (1.4968), Kent (0.8578), Midland (1.5), Monroe (0.9866), Muskegon (0.9749), Ottawa (0.8616), and Charlevoix-Emmet (0.953); 44% of Michigan students receive enhancement-millage funding.
- Projected Oakland County per-pupil revenue rises from $728.04 (Year 1) to $835.84 (Year 6); total revenue from $125.8M to $144.4M.

Stated uses / position
- Competitive compensation, staff recruitment/retention, staffing supports, professional development, lower family out-of-pocket costs, class sizes, safety and wellness, special-education funding stability, and district-wide programming and transportation.
- The Board frames its resolution as 'letting voters decide' and explicitly not an endorsement of the millage.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
An informational slide presentation prepared for the Troy Board of Education explaining a proposed Oakland County regional enhancement millage to be placed before voters on Tuesday, August 4, 2026.

What an enhancement millage is: Since 1994's Proposal A, the State of Michigan controls school operating funding, with the regional enhancement millage as the sole exception. Constituent school districts representing at least 51% of the intermediate district's total student population must submit affirmative requests to Oakland Schools; the proposal must be made on a county-wide basis and passes or fails county-wide rather than by local community. If approved, the money is collected by the ISD and distributed equally to all public-school districts and public-school academies on a per-pupil basis, with each district retaining local control over how the money is spent.

Existing millages: The presentation lists nine counties that already levy an enhancement millage - Wayne (1.9812 mills, ~$360/student; approved 2016, renewed November 2020 and November 2024), Macomb (1.8305 mills, ~$400/student; approved March 2020), Charlevoix-Emmet (0.953 mills), Kalamazoo (1.4968 mills), Kent (0.8578 mills), Midland (1.5 mills), Monroe (0.9866 mills), Muskegon (0.9749 mills), and Ottawa (0.8616 mills). It states that 44% of Michigan students receive enhancement-millage funding.

The proposal: 1.5 mills levied over six years, generating approximately $781 per pupil annually (about $4,686 per pupil over the six-year period) for each Oakland County public-school student. It would cost approximately $300 per year on a Troy home valued at $400,000 (taxable value $200,000), and collection would begin in December 2026. Projected Oakland County per-pupil revenue by year: Year 1 $728.04, Year 2 $748.42, Year 3 $769.38, Year 4 $790.92, Year 5 $813.07, Year 6 $835.84; corresponding total revenue: $125.8M, $129.3M, $132.9M, $136.7M, $140.5M, $144.4M.

Timeline and process: Local resolutions must be adopted within a 180-day period and transmitted to Oakland Schools; the Oakland Schools Board of Education then adopts a resolution certifying the ballot-proposal text to the Oakland County Clerk (the 'School District Election Coordinator'), with copies to the local clerks and other affected county clerks; the election date is Tuesday, August 4, 2026. A case study cites a Michigan School Board Association presentation, 'Enhancement Millages: Successes, Challenges, Planning for the Future,' featuring Kent ISD, East Grand Rapids Public Schools, and Rockford Public Schools.

Stated district benefits and uses: making compensation more competitive, attracting and retaining talented staff, maintaining staffing supports, providing additional professional development, decreasing out-of-pocket costs for families, maintaining class sizes, continued focus on student safety and wellness, stabilizing special-education funding, and maintaining district-wide programming and transportation - framed against 'cost outpacing funding.' The closing slide, 'Resolution: Let Voters Decide,' states that the Board's resolution is not an endorsement of the millage itself but is intended to empower the community to make informed decisions and to ensure democratic participation and transparency.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
An executive-summary slide deck for the Troy School District 'AI Guidance 2026 Edition,' presenting the district's approach to artificial intelligence in K-12 instruction.

Vision & beliefs
- AI enhances learning, not replaces thinking
- AI literacy is foundational (K-12)
- Teachers maintain instructional authority
- Student data privacy is non-negotiable
- AI aligns with the Portrait of a Graduate and UDL

Governance & guardrails
- Board Policy 8001 and the Acceptable Use Policy
- Approved platforms: Microsoft Copilot and Magic School
- FERPA, COPPA, and CIPA compliance
- No personally identifiable information (PII) in public AI platforms
- Academic integrity expectations remain

0 to Infinity classroom framework
Defines the permitted level of AI involvement so students preserve originality and disclose use:
- Level 0 - AI Free: in-class assessment, no AI; accessibility/UDL tools only
- Level 1 - AI Assisted: brainstorming, guiding questions, outlines (Magic School Prompt Creator, Story Web, Idea Generator)
- Level 2 - AI Enhanced: explanations and summaries, cross-referenced for bias (Explainer, Research Assistant, Character Chatbot)
- Level 3 - AI Empowered: project descriptions, images, data analysis (Data Analyzer, Presentation Designer)

Implementation
Elementary use is teacher-directed and scaffolded; secondary use is structured and teacher-guided. Five hours of district-wide AI professional development have been completed, with job-embedded training in Grades 3-5, building-level sharing by tech chairs and principals, and family partnership.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
An executive-summary presentation titled 'TSD AI Guidance 2026 Edition,' summarizing the Troy School District's framework for the use of artificial intelligence across K-12 instruction.

Vision and beliefs: The district states that AI should enhance learning rather than replace thinking; that AI literacy is foundational across K-12; that teachers maintain instructional authority; that student data privacy is non-negotiable; and that AI use aligns with the district's Portrait of a Graduate and Universal Design for Learning (UDL).

Governance and guardrails: Governance is anchored in Board Policy 8001 and the district's Acceptable Use Policy. The two approved platforms are Microsoft Copilot and Magic School. Use must comply with FERPA, COPPA, and CIPA; no personally identifiable information (PII) may be entered into public AI platforms; and academic integrity expectations remain in force.

AI literacy and instructional integration: Students are to learn how AI works and its limits, how to critically evaluate AI outputs, how to protect privacy and use AI ethically, and how to maintain ownership of their thinking. Elementary use is teacher-directed and scaffolded, while secondary use is structured and teacher-guided.

0 to Infinity classroom integration framework: This framework defines the permitted level of AI involvement in student work, preserving student originality, clarifying expectations before work begins, reducing ambiguity, and supporting differentiation. Students must follow the designated AI level and disclose their use. The levels, with example tools, are:
- Level 0 - AI Free: in-class assessments completed in class or on paper, with no AI brainstorming or drafting; only accessibility/UDL tools such as dictation and translation are permitted.
- Level 1 - AI Assisted: students brainstorm topics, generate guiding questions, and create outline prompts using tools such as Magic School Prompt Creator, MS Story Web, MS Idea Generator, and MS 5 Questions.
- Level 2 - AI Enhanced: students generate simple explanations and summaries (for example, historical causes) and cross-reference for bias and oversimplification using tools such as Magic School Explainer, MS Research Assistant, and MS Character Chatbot.
- Level 3 - AI Empowered: students create project descriptions and images and analyze data using MS Data Analyzer and MS Presentation Designer.

Professional learning and continuous review: The district reports five hours of district-wide AI professional development completed, with job-embedded training in Grades 3-5, ongoing updates as tools and regulations evolve, building-level sharing by technology chairs and principals, and family partnership and communication - framed as balancing innovation with responsibility. The deck also references classroom examples of Magic School in use.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A pupil enrollment projection study prepared for the Troy School District by Plante Moran Realpoint (Cresa) in February 2026 and presented at the Board's March 7 winter retreat. It documents the demographic trends underlying enrollment, showing that while the district's total population grew between 2020 and 2025 and is projected to rise slightly through 2030, that population is aging, with the under-18 share shrinking as the 65-and-over share expands. Oakland County births declined from about 13,454 in 2014 to a projected 12,233 in 2025.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
A pupil enrollment projection study for the Troy School District prepared by Plante Moran Realpoint (Cresa), dated February 2026 and presented at the March 7, 2026 Winter Board of Education Retreat. It is organized into Section 1 (Demographics) and Section 2 (Districtwide Pupil Enrollment Projections); the extracted text covers the demographic section.

Key demographic findings
- Births: Oakland County births fell from roughly 13,454 (2014) to a projected 12,233 (2025); kindergarten enrollment runs about 5.2%-6.1% of births. Michigan births are also declining, and 2024 figures are provisional.
- Regional trend: 171 of 233 communities in the region saw a decreased birth rate between 2002 and 2020.
- Population: the district's total population was higher in 2025 than 2020 and is projected to grow slightly through 2030 (chart spans roughly 55,000-73,000).
- Aging: the under-18 share of population is shrinking while the 65-and-over share has grown significantly; the population is described as growing and aging.
- School choice: district public schools hold a lower share than private for preschool but a higher share for every other grade cohort; public-school share rose slightly from 2020 to 2025.
- Income: the share of households earning under $100K has fallen while the $100K-plus share (especially $250K-plus) has grown, a trend projected to continue to 2030.

Purpose
To give the Board demographic context (births, migration, aging, income, and housing values) that drives the district's multi-year enrollment forecasts used for budget and staffing planning.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Prepared by Plante Moran Realpoint (also referenced as Plante Moran Cresa) and dated February 2026, the Pupil Enrollment Projection Study was presented to the Troy School District Board of Education at its Winter Retreat on March 7, 2026. The study is divided into Section 1, Demographics, and Section 2, Districtwide Pupil Enrollment Projections; the extracted text primarily covers the demographic foundation for the enrollment forecast.

Births and kindergarten conversion: The report tracks Michigan and Oakland County births, noting that 2024 births are provisional and 2025 births are projected. Oakland County births declined from 13,454 (2014), 13,547 (2015) and 13,627 (2016) toward figures around 12,298 (2020), 12,877 (2021), 12,449 (2022), 12,029 (2023) and a projected 12,233 for 2024 and 2025. Kindergarten population as a share of births (K% Birth) ranges from about 5.2% to 6.1% across birth years 2014-2025.

Regional context: While Southeast Michigan is experiencing an aging population and reduced birth rates, patterns differ by community. Nearly three quarters of communities, 171 of 233, in the region saw a decrease in birth rate between 2002 and 2020. The study references an in-depth analysis of forecasted changes in the region's school-age population (children aged 5 to 17) over the next 30 years, highlighting continued aging, fewer births, migration as a factor in population change, and local trends affecting individual districts.

Troy population trends: The district had more residents in 2025 than in 2020 and is projected to grow its population slightly through 2030 (the total-population chart spans roughly 55,000 to 73,000). Distribution by age has shifted: the population under 18 represents a smaller share of the total in 2025 than in 2010, while the 65-and-over share has increased significantly; these trends are projected to continue through 2030. The report summarizes the district as growing and aging.

School enrollment patterns: Comparing public versus private enrollment for the district, Oakland County, and the state, the district's public schools hold a lower share of students than private schools for preschool, but a higher share for every other cohort. Public-school enrollment share increased slightly for each cohort in the district between 2020 and 2025.

Household income and housing: The distribution of households by income has shifted upward. The share of households earning less than $100K decreased while the share earning more than $100K increased, indicating rising incomes; this trend is projected to continue into 2030, particularly for the highest bracket of $250K and above. The report also begins presenting owner-occupied housing units by value for 2020, 2025, and 2030 (text truncated). Together these indicators inform the district's multi-year, districtwide enrollment projections used for budget and staffing planning.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A four-year General Fund forecast for the Troy School District dated February 2026 and presented at the Board's March 7 winter retreat. Operating expenditures outpace operating revenues in every year, producing operating deficits of roughly $5.1M to $12.1M, and the ending fund balance is projected to erode from $33.7M (17.41% of expenditures) to $28.1M (14.17%) by 2028-29.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
An administration presentation delivered at the Troy School District Winter Retreat, March 7, 2026, covering General Fund Budget Amendment #2 (2025-2026) and the strategy for balancing the FY2026-27 budget.

Amendment #2 figures (Original / Amend #1 / Amend #2)
- Revenue: $190,545,984 / $197,760,255 / $201,232,225
- Expenditures: $194,285,613 / $203,763,818 / $206,832,475
