To affirm budget priorities and reduction targets and gather Board feedback before finalizing FY2026-27 cuts.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Presented by the administration at the Troy School District Winter Retreat on March 7, 2026, this Board presentation had four stated objectives: provide a clear overview of the district's financial status and the factors affecting the budget; ensure board members understand and affirm budget priorities and reduction targets; review a budget reduction recommendation matrix; and solicit Board feedback.

General Fund Budget Amendment #2 (2025-2026) reflects four categories of change: (1) minor revenue adjustments to align with the February 2026 State Aid Status Report; (2) revenue and expenditure adjustments so the general ledger matches all submitted and approved grant applications; (3) salary and benefit adjustments reflecting current staffing levels, including several mid-year retirements and vacancies; and (4) amended non-salary, non-benefit expenditures reflecting year-to-date plus projected costs.

Comparing the Original Budget, Amendment #1, and Amendment #2: revenue moves from $190,545,984 to $197,760,255 to $201,232,225; expenditures from $194,285,613 to $203,763,818 to $206,832,475; change in fund balance from -$3,739,629 to -$6,003,563 to -$5,600,250; beginning fund balance $32,979,691 then $33,713,795; ending fund balance $29,240,062, $27,710,232, and $28,113,545; and fund balance percentage 15.05%, 13.59%, and 13.59%.

Revenue adjustments between Amendment #1 and #2 include enrollment easing from 12,071.23 to 12,068.58 FTE (-2.65), 27h(2) Mentoring +$363,038, 27l(2) Educator Comp +$1,784,862, 31aa Mental/Safety rising from $1,966,318 to $3,797,147 (+$1,830,829), and Other Grants +$212,834. Matching expenditure adjustments include the same 27h(2), 27l(2) and Other Grants amounts, plus Edustaff rising from $8,696,899 to $9,054,655 (+$357,756) and Facility Supplies from $1,134,200 to $1,314,000 (+$179,800).

The 2026-2027 Original Budget estimate assumes revenue of $201,418,960 and expenditures of $199,580,639, producing a positive change of $1,838,321, an ending fund balance of $29,951,866, and a 15.01% fund balance.

Budgetary challenges cited are enrollment, lack of urgency in Lansing, the revenue landscape, rising expenditures, salary and benefits, retirement costs, and special education. Budget priorities are to secure known expenditure obligations through 2029 (enabling multi-year projections, labor stability, and morale), to pursue data-driven alignment of student support services (support for MTSS teams K-12, development of a K-8 reading curriculum, and continued math implementation), and to make reductions through attrition where feasible, a strategy used over the prior three years to avoid layoffs. The presentation notes 95% of the budget is people, that reductions in force (RIF) would be viewed through the lens of least impact on student achievement, and that a possible Employee Severance Plan would be reviewed.

The budget process gathers input from multiple work groups including SSAB, principals, administrative staff, and sub-cabinet. Reduction targets are to maintain instructional priorities, achieve structural balance, and preserve a 15% fund balance, with a proposed roughly $12 million in reductions across salaries and benefits, purchased services, departmental adjustments, and discretionary spending. Proposed reductions focus on positions not directly connected to the classroom, maximizing adult-to-student ratios and contract allowances, and realigning administrative and support staffing.

The proposed budget timeline runs from the January 13 workshop (Amendment #1; CREC on 1/16), the February 3 workshop (Plante Moran Cresa enrollment projections; the Governor's Executive Budget and February 25 State of the State), the March 7 retreat (Amendment #2), an April workshop (reduction recommendations), and a June regular meeting (Amendment #3, the FY26-27 Budget Resolution, and final RIF targets).

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A one-page statement of the Troy School District's guiding principles for selecting furniture in future-ready learning environments, presented at the March 7, 2026 winter retreat. It sets out five principles: furniture should support movement and motion; inspire student agency and healthy risk-taking; be comfortable and foster belonging; meet the needs of all students and staff; and encourage innovative pedagogy. Each principle is expanded with five supporting criteria emphasizing flexibility, comfort, inclusivity, and collaboration.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
A single-page guiding-principles document titled TSD Guiding Principles for Furniture in Future-Ready Learning Environments, presented at the Troy School District Winter Board of Education Retreat on March 7, 2026. It frames the criteria the district uses to evaluate classroom furniture, connected to its building projects.

The five principles
1. Supports movement and motion: easy to move, pairs with other pieces for multiple configurations, encourages students to move, allows comfortable proximity to others, and aids efficient transitions.
2. Supports and inspires student agency and healthy risk-taking: builds self-awareness, can be used in many (even unexpected) ways, sustains engagement, lets students show their work, and supports organization and access to tools.
3. Comfortable and fosters a sense of belonging: provides a feeling of safety, is considered comfortable by most, empowers students to organize furniture purposefully, makes the space exciting and joyful, and supports a variety of postures.
4. Meets the needs of all students and staff: promotes community (ours, not mine), supports bodies of all sizes and abilities, creates a positive sensory experience, lets teachers work alongside students, and is adjustable on demand.
5. Encourages and supports innovative pedagogy: enables whole-group instruction, partner work, individual worktime, small-group collaboration, and student voice.

Purpose
To provide a shared, student-centered rubric for furniture selection as the district equips new and renovated learning spaces.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Titled TSD Guiding Principles for Furniture in Future-Ready Learning Environments, this single-page Troy School District document was presented at the Winter Board of Education Retreat on March 7, 2026. It enumerates five guiding principles, each with five supporting criteria, that define what the district values when selecting classroom furniture, context that connects to the district's building projects and new learning spaces.

Principle 1, Furniture that supports movement and motion: it should be able to move around the room easily; partner with other furniture pieces to support multiple configurations; encourage students to move their bodies; allow students to find a comfortable proximity to others; and aid efficient transitions.

Principle 2, Furniture that supports and inspires student agency and healthy risk-taking: it should support self-awareness and be chosen to support learning needs; be usable in many different and even unexpected ways; increase students' ability to sustain engagement; empower students to show their work; and support students in their organization and access to tools.

Principle 3, Furniture that is comfortable and fosters a sense of belonging: it should give students a feeling of safety; be considered comfortable by most; empower students to work together to organize the furniture purposefully; make the space feel exciting and joyful; and support a variety of student postures.

Principle 4, Furniture that meets the needs of all students and staff: it should promote a sense of community (not mine but ours); support bodies of all sizes and abilities; create a positive sensory experience; facilitate teachers working alongside students; and be adjustable on-demand.

Principle 5, Furniture that encourages and supports innovative pedagogy: it should provide access to whole-group instruction; choice in partner work; choice in individual worktime; small-group gathering and collaboration; and elicit student voice and the sharing of ideas.

Together, the principles articulate a student-centered, flexible, and inclusive standard intended to guide purchasing decisions for future-ready learning environments across the district.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
The administration's presentation deck supporting General Fund Budget Amendment #2 for fiscal year 2025-2026, Troy School District, prepared for the Board (agenda item 5.D) and dated March 2026.

Rationale for the amendment (four drivers): (1) minor adjustments to revenues to align with the district's February 2026 State Aid Status Report; (2) revenue and expenditure adjustments so the general ledger matches all submitted and approved grant applications; (3) salary and benefit adjustments to reflect the most recent staffing levels, factoring in several mid-year retirements and vacancies; and (4) amended non-salary and non-benefit expenditures reflecting year-to-date spending plus projected remaining expenses.

General Fund trajectory (Original -> Amendment #1 -> Amendment #2): Revenue $190,545,984 -> $197,760,255 -> $201,232,225; Expenditures $194,285,613 -> $203,763,818 -> $206,832,475; Change in Fund Balance ($3,739,629) -> ($6,003,563) -> ($5,600,250); Beginning Fund Balance $32,979,691 -> $33,713,795 -> $33,713,795; Ending Fund Balance $29,240,062 -> $27,710,232 -> $28,113,545; Fund Balance percentage 15.05% -> 13.59% -> 13.59%.

Revenue adjustments (Amendment #1 -> #2): enrollment 12,071.23 -> 12,068.58 (down 2.65); 27h(2) Mentoring $0 -> $363,038; 27l(2) Educator Comp $0 -> $1,784,862; 31aa Mental/Safety $1,966,318 -> $3,797,147 (up $1,830,829); Other Grants $4,929,485 -> $5,142,319 (up $212,834). Expenditure adjustments mirror the grant additions and include Edustaff $8,696,899 -> $9,054,655 (up $357,756) and Facility Supplies $1,134,200 -> $1,314,000 (up $179,800).

FY 2026-27 original-budget estimate (vs. Amendment #2): Revenue $201,418,960; Expenditures $199,580,639; Change in Fund Balance +$1,838,321; Beginning Fund Balance $28,113,545; Ending Fund Balance $29,951,866; Fund Balance percentage 15.01%.

Budgetary challenges cited: enrollment, 'lack of urgency in Lansing,' the revenue landscape, rising expenditures, salary and benefits, retirement costs, and special education. Budget priorities: securing known expenditure obligations through 2029 to enable multi-year projections, labor stability, and morale; data-driven alignment of student support services (support for MTSS teams K-12, development and implementation of a K-8 reading curriculum, and continued math implementation and student support); and reductions through attrition where feasible, noting the approach has been used over the last three years to avoid layoffs, that 95% of the budget is people, that reductions in force would be viewed through 'least impact on student achievement,' and that a possible Employee Severance Plan would be reviewed.

Budget process and reduction targets: input gathered from multiple work groups (SSAB, principals, administrative staff, sub-cabinet); a reduction framework with a scoring rubric; proposed targets of about $12 million in reductions across salaries and benefits, purchased services, departmental adjustments, and discretionary spending; maintaining structural balance and a 15% fund balance. Areas for consideration include positions not directly connected to the classroom, maximizing adult-to-student ratios and contract allowances, and realigning administrative and support staffing.

Board feedback was sought on whether the priorities and targets align with Board expectations. Proposed budget timeline: January workshop (1/13/26, Amendment #1, CREC 1/16); February workshop (2/3/26, enrollment projections by Plante Moran Cresa, Governor's Executive Budget); March retreat (3/7/26, Amendment #2); April workshop (reduction recommendations); and the June regular meeting (Amendment #3 and the FY 26-27 Budget Resolution, including final RIF targets).

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A consent-agenda item for the March 17, 2026 Troy Board of Education meeting recommending that seven schools be closed to open enrollment for 2026-2027. Barnard, Bemis, Schroeder, Boulan Park, and Larson Schools would close due to enrollment and physical space constraints, while Athens and Troy High would close except for up to 25 incoming ninth graders residing in the Troy High attendance area who wish to attend Athens High. Applications for those 25 seats would be accepted during a two-week window in March.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
Consent-agenda item 5.E for the Troy Board of Education Regular Meeting of March 17, 2026, recommending a resolution on schools closed to open enrollment for the 2026-2027 school year.

Recommendation
Administration reviewed enrollment across elementary, middle, and high school attendance areas. Based on building enrollment totals and physical space constraints, it recommends closing the following to open enrollment:
- Barnard, Bemis, Schroeder, Boulan Park, and Larson Schools
- Athens High School and Troy High School

Exception
Athens and Troy High have been closed for several years to maximize each building's enrollment. For 2026-2027, an exception allows not more than 25 incoming ninth-grade students who reside in the Troy High School attendance area but wish to attend Athens High School. Applications for these 25 spots will be accepted during a two-week window in March. Students with siblings attending Athens and Troy High who are currently enrolled in grades 9-11 will be allowed to open enroll to remain for 2026-2027.

Action
Recommended action is to adopt the suggested resolution, with blank lines for the mover, supporter, and Yes/No vote counts.

Purpose
Manages enrollment and capacity across Troy School District buildings by limiting open-enrollment entry where space is constrained.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Consent-agenda item 5.E, dated 03.17.26, presented to the Troy Board of Education at its Regular Meeting of the Board of Education (7:00 PM) on March 17, 2026, under the Consent section. Administration reported that it had reviewed the enrollment for the elementary, middle, and high school attendance areas.

Because of total student enrollment and physical space constraints at the elementary and middle school buildings, administration recommended that Barnard, Bemis, Schroeder, Boulan Park, and Larson Schools be closed to open enrollment. For the high schools, the stated goal for Athens and Troy High has been to maximize each building's enrollment, which has resulted in both schools being closed to open enrollment for the past several years. Based on current enrollment projections for 2026-2027, administration recommended that Athens and Troy High also be closed to open enrollment, with one exception: not more than twenty-five (25) incoming ninth-grade students who reside in the Troy High School attendance area but wish to attend Athens High School. Applications for the 25 spots at Athens High School would be accepted during a two-week window in March.

The recommended action was to adopt the resolution. The suggested resolution reads: BE IT THEREFORE RESOLVED that the Troy Board of Education adopts a resolution to close Barnard, Bemis, Schroeder, Boulan Park, and Larson Schools as well as Athens and Troy High Schools to open enrollment for the 2026-2027 school year, with the exception of not more than twenty-five (25) incoming ninth-grade students who reside in the Troy High School attendance area but wish to attend Athens High School. The resolution further provides that students with siblings attending Athens and Troy High and currently enrolled in grades 9-11 will be allowed to open enroll to remain for the 2026-2027 school year.

The document includes blank fields for the mover, the supporter, and the Yes/No vote tally, indicating the resolution had not yet been voted at the time of the packet.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A February 2026 Pupil Enrollment Projection Study prepared for the Troy School District by Plante Moran Realpoint, presented as agenda item 8.A at the March 17, 2026 Board of Education meeting. The report covers demographics and districtwide enrollment projections, documenting declining Michigan and Oakland County births, a growing but aging Troy population projected to expand slightly through 2030, and rising household incomes. It notes that 171 of 233 communities in the region saw birth-rate decreases between 2002 and 2020.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
A Pupil Enrollment Projection Study for the Troy School District dated February 2026, prepared by Plante Moran Realpoint and presented as agenda item 8.A at the Regular Meeting of the Board of Education on March 17, 2026. The excerpt covers Section 1 (Demographics) and introduces Section 2 (Districtwide Pupil Enrollment Projections).

Demographic findings
- Michigan and Oakland County births are declining; Oakland County births fell from about 13,454 (2014) toward roughly 12,233 (2024-2025 projected), with kindergarten capture running about 5.2-6.1% of births.
- 171 of 233 communities in the region (nearly three quarters) saw a birth-rate decrease between 2002 and 2020.
- The study includes a 30-year forecast of the region's school-age population (ages 5-17) and cites Southeast Michigan trends: an aging population, fewer births, and migration.

Troy-specific trends
- The district's total population was higher in 2025 than 2020 and is projected to grow slightly through 2030; the population is described as growing and aging, with the under-18 share shrinking and the 65-and-over share rising.
- Public-school enrollment share increased slightly for each cohort from 2020 to 2025.
- Household incomes are rising: the share of households earning under $100K fell while higher brackets grew, especially $250K+.

Purpose
Informs district planning on facilities, staffing, and capacity by projecting future enrollment from demographic and housing data.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A Pupil Enrollment Projection Study for the Troy School District, dated February 2026 and prepared by Plante Moran Realpoint, presented as agenda item 8.A at the Troy Board of Education Regular Meeting of the Board of Education (7:00 PM) on March 17, 2026. The study is organized into Section 1 (Demographics) and Section 2 (Pupil Enrollment Projections -- Districtwide).

Demographics. The report opens with statewide and county birth data. Michigan total births are trending down (2024 figures noted as provisional). For Oakland County, births by year run approximately 13,454 (2014), 13,547 (2015), 13,627 (2016), 13,184 (2017), 13,152 (2018), 12,899 (2019), 12,298 (2020), 12,877 (2021), 12,449 (2022), 12,029 (2023), and 12,233 (2024 provisional; 2025 projected) -- a general decline. Kindergarten population as a percentage of births ('K% Birth') ranges roughly 5.2% to 6.1% across those years. The report notes that nearly three quarters of communities in the region -- 171 out of 233 -- saw a decrease in birth rate between 2002 and 2020.

The study includes an in-depth analysis of forecasted changes in the region's school-age population (children aged 5 to 17) over the next 30 years and its impacts on K-12 education. It identifies four Southeast Michigan trends: the continued aging of the region, fewer births, migration as a factor in population change, and local trends impacting individual school districts. A regional map categorizes districts by projected gain or loss (for example, 'More than 1,000 Loss,' '501 to 1,000 Loss,' up to 'More than 500 Gain').

Troy School District specifics. Total population in the district was higher in 2025 than in 2020, and the district is projected to grow its population slightly through 2030. The population-by-age distribution shows the under-18 share declining while the 65-and-over share rises significantly; across 2010, 2020, 2025, and 2030 the 65+ cohort grows from about 13% to roughly 21%, while the 18-and-under share falls from about 26% to 21%. The report summarizes that the district's population is 'growing and aging.'

School enrollment trends compare public versus private enrollment for school-aged children in the district, Oakland County, and the state. Within the district, public schools have a lower share than private for preschool but a higher share for every other cohort, and public-school enrollment share increased slightly for each cohort from 2020 to 2025.

Household income and housing. Households-by-income data for 2020, 2025, and 2030 show the share of households earning less than $100K decreasing while the share earning more than $100K increases, indicating rising incomes; this trend is projected to continue to 2030, particularly for the highest bracket ($250K+). For example, the $250K+ share moves from about 13% (2020) to 14% (2025) to 19% (2030), while lower brackets such as under $25,000 (8% to 5%) and $25,000-$49,999 (11% to 7%) decline. The excerpt ends as it begins presenting owner-occupied housing units by value for 2020, 2025, and 2030 (text truncated).

The study's purpose is to give the district and community a data-grounded basis for enrollment forecasting and facilities and capacity planning, drawing on births, migration, public/private enrollment splits, household income, and housing value.

What it is
A 'Letter of Explanation' for the Corridor & P.E. Locker Category of the Boulan Park Renovation Project (RFP 2526-21), supporting agenda item 8.C at the March 17, 2026 Board meeting. It explains why the locker-category recommendation was revised to Rayhaven Group.

Original bid scope
Per the RFP specifications, existing corridor lockers were to be removed, stored, and reinstalled, while P.E. lockers were to be demolished and replaced with new lockers. Steel Equipment Co. was the only bidder to bid that exact scope. The other two bidders submitted a voluntary alternative: install new corridor lockers (with new locks) and new P.E. lockers.

Why the change
Operations cited multiple existing locker repairs and needed lock replacements, concerns about locker condition after removal/storage/reinstallation, anticipated modifications, and past contractor performance issues regarding quality, reliability, and warranty support. For these reasons, the author could not recommend Steel Equipment Co. as the low qualified bidder.

Recommendation
Proceed with the next low bidder, Rayhaven Group, to provide and install new corridor lockers with new Master Combination Locks / Electronic Digital Locks (for Special Ed) and new P.E. lockers per its alternate bid. Post-bid interviews produced an approved revised non-welded corridor locker that improves future maintainability and yields an estimated additional savings of $69,200. The BOND Construction Team reviewed and approved the revised option.

Cost note
The revision provides all-new corridor lockers and locks for an estimated $100K more than reusing the existing lockers (with their existing issues) via a contractor with past performance concerns.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A 'Letter of Explanation' concerning the Corridor & P.E. Locker Category/Purchase within the Boulan Park Renovation Project (RFP 2526-21), supporting agenda item 8.C at the Troy Board of Education Regular Meeting of March 17, 2026. It documents and justifies a revision of the locker-category award, with the recommended contractor now Rayhaven Group.

Original scope and bids. Under the RFP bid specifications, the existing corridor lockers were scheduled for removal, storage, and reinstallation, while the P.E. lockers were scheduled for demolition and replacement with new lockers (purchase and installation). Steel Equipment Co. was the only bidder that bid that specified scope. The other two bidders provided a voluntary alternative bid to install new corridor lockers (with new locks) and new P.E. lockers rather than reinstalling the old corridor lockers.

Rationale for not recommending the low bidder. After further discussion of existing locker conditions -- including multiple locker repairs and lock replacements that Operations found needed or recommended due to current issues -- as well as anticipated modifications, concerns about locker condition after removal, storage, and reinstallation, and past contractor performance issues regarding quality, reliability, and warranty support, the author states he cannot recommend Steel Equipment Co. as the low qualified bidder.

Recommendation. The letter recommends proceeding with the next low bidder, Rayhaven Group, to provide and install new corridor lockers fitted with new Master Combination Locks / Electronic Digital Locks (the latter for Special Ed) and new P.E. lockers, per Rayhaven's alternate bid proposal. During the post-bid interview, further discussion and clarifications resulted in an approved and revised non-welded locker for the corridors; this design gives Operations more flexibility to maintain the lockers in the future and carries an estimated additional savings of $69,200.00. The revised option was reviewed and approved by the district's BOND Construction Team.

Cost trade-off. The category revision results in all-new corridor lockers and locks for an estimated $100K more than the alternative of using the existing lockers (with their existing issues and repairs) supplied through a contractor with past performance issues. The author frames the revised decision as the best value for the Troy School District, reached through the post-bid interviews and extended discussions. In the companion award recommendation, the Lockers category is listed at $272,700 (Rayhaven Group).

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A March 17, 2026 resolution asking the Board to award the complete renovation of Boulan Park Middle School — architectural, mechanical, electrical, and structural work — for a total of $20,185,066 from the Capital Projects Fund. The award covers $18,350,066 in category contracts plus a 10% ($1,835,000) contingency, following a competitive RFP reviewed by Operations Director Rob Carson and the Barton Malow Company.

Action requested
Under Business item 8.C, the Board is asked to accept a resolution awarding the complete renovation of Boulan Park Middle School and to approve the expenditure from the Capital Projects Fund.

Process
An RFP was issued for competitive bids covering architectural, mechanical, electrical, and structural work. Responses were reviewed by Rob Carson, Director of Operations, together with the Barton Malow Company, which recommended the awards below.

Award
Category awards total $18,350,066, with a 10% contingency of $1,835,000, for a total recommended award of $20,185,066.

Demolition — North American Dismantling Corp. ($1,306,350); Concrete — Metropolitan Concrete Corp. Purpose
This is the suggested resolution for Business item 8.C at the March 17, 2026 regular meeting: consideration of the Boulan Park Renovation Project. It asks the Board to award a complete renovation of Boulan Park Middle School — encompassing architectural, mechanical, electrical, and structural work — and to approve the total as an expenditure of the Capital Projects Fund.

Procurement process
An RFP was issued to obtain competitive bids for the full renovation. Bid responses were reviewed by Rob Carson, the district's Director of Operations, in conjunction with the Barton Malow Company (construction manager), which produced the award recommendation. The resolution is drafted in standard form with mover/supporter and yes/no lines to be completed on the floor.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A March 12, 2026 revised memo from Director of Maintenance & Operations Rob Carson to Assistant Superintendent Dan Trudel recommending award of Bid 2526-22, the Troy High School stadium paving and track replacement (agenda item 8.D). The three-category project replaces the stadium's asphalt, running track, and fencing due to age and condition, awarding Nationwide Construction Group, Dalco Services, and Al's Asphalt Paving for a total project cost of $1,426,070.80. A memorandum from the Troy School District Operations Department (1140 Rankin, Troy, MI 48083; Ph 248.823.4050, Fax 248.823.4077), dated March 12, 2026, from Rob Carson, Director of Maintenance & Operations, to Dan Trudel, Assistant Superintendent of Business Services. It is the revised (March 2026) recommendation supporting agenda item 8.D for the Regular Meeting of the Board of Education (7:00 PM) on March 17, 2026, and concerns Bid 2526-22, the THS Stadium Paving & Track Replacement Project.

Scope and rationale. A Request for Proposals was issued to obtain competitive bids for the Troy High Stadium pavement and running track replacement. The scope of work is to replace the existing asphalt pavement, running track, and fencing in the stadium per the bid specification. The replacements are planned due to age and condition. The project comprises three bid categories; a bid summary and the Barton Malow Builders contractor recommendation were attached for review, and post-bid interviews were conducted to verify the accuracy and thoroughness of the contractor bids.

Recommended contractors (low qualified bidder for each category): Fencing -- Nationwide Construction Group -- $143,862.00; Site Work -- Dalco Services -- $483,000.00; Asphalt & Surfacing -- Al's Asphalt Paving -- $669,566.00. The Apparent Low Contractor Award Total is $1,296,428.00, with a Project Contingency (10%) of $129,642.80, for a Total Project Award Cost of $1,426,070.80.

Funding and schedule. Funding for this purchase will come from the Capital Improvements Bond Fund and the Building Site & Sinking Fund. The intent is to start the project in mid-May, with completion by August 8, 2026.

Routing. Copies (Cc) were sent to Donna Havrilla in the Business Department and to the Purchasing Department file. This memo, together with the Barton Malow Builders award-recommendation letter dated March 10, 2026 and the board resolution for the same project, forms the district's basis for awarding the stadium paving and track replacement; the resolution approves the $1,426,070.80 expenditure from the Building Site & Sinking Fund and the Capital Bonds Fund.
